input_references.role: Vessel type, name, dimensions, and fishing-vessel home harbour linked by vessel_id
Main and small harbour reference locations
Two typical official transit-route reference trajectories (A and E)

metadata.goal: To detect and investigate movement patterns of fishing vessels with given trajectories of fishing vessels and other type vessels in this area.
metadata.category: Kattegat fishing activity, vessel size, and route adherence
metadata.header: Kattegat Fishing Harbours, Vessel Size, and Official-Route Avoidance
metadata.dataset_description: This derived case uses AIS-like position, time, speed, and course fields consistent with the Section 9.1 AIS description, together with vessel attributes, harbour locations, and report-line-style A/E route references. Section 9.4 identifies Anholt, Bønnerup, and Grenaa as the main fishing harbours, notes the predominance of smaller vessels, and describes fishing sailing patterns as more random than larger-vessel traffic because fishing vessels do not follow official routes. The concrete trajectories and small-harbour calls are for this case.
metadata.source_note: Raw 2026 Danish AIS provides the field structure; the case interpretation is based on risk_to_ship_traffic.pdf Sections 9.1 and 9.4.

insight_list.insight: Three main harbours structure fishing activity in the selected sea area: Anholt, Bønnerup, and Grenaa. They account for 33 of 36 observed fishing-trip endpoints, whereas the supplied small harbours receive only occasional calls.

plot.title: Fishing Activity by Harbour
plot.description: Harbour-circle size encodes trajectory endpoints; the three repeatedly used ports contrast with occasional calls at the small harbours.

insight_list.question: Which harbours anchor the fishing-vessel activity, and how concentrated are the observed fishing-trip endpoints among them?

insight_list.insight: Fishing vessels are predominantly small: 15 of 18 fishing vessels are shorter than 15 m, while only three are larger fishing vessels.

insight_list.insight: Fishing-vessel trajectories are far more spatially dispersed than the larger cargo and tanker trajectories. The larger vessels closely follow the supplied A and E official transit references, whereas fishing vessels repeatedly move between nearshore grounds and harbours and do not consistently align with either corridor.

insights: Three main harbours structure fishing activity in the selected sea area: Anholt, Bønnerup, and Grenaa. They account for 33 of 36 observed fishing-trip endpoints, whereas the supplied small harbours receive only occasional calls.
Fishing vessels are predominantly small: 15 of 18 fishing vessels are shorter than 15 m, while only three are larger fishing vessels.

Fishing-vessel trajectories are far more spatially dispersed than the larger cargo and tanker trajectories. The larger vessels closely follow the supplied A and E official transit references, whereas fishing vessels repeatedly move between nearshore grounds and harbours and do not consistently align with either corridor.
summary: Fishing activity in the selected Kattegat area is concentrated around Anholt, Bønnerup, and Grenaa, and most fishing vessels are small. Unlike the provided cargo and tanker movements, fishing trajectories disperse among nearshore grounds and harbour calls rather than closely tracking the two official transit corridors.
